questions.question: In which year did Babur defeat the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat and capture Delhi and Agra?
questions.questionHtml: In which year did Babur defeat the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat and capture Delhi and Agra?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1526.

  • In 1526, Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and captured Delhi and Agra.
  • This is called The first battle of Panipat.
  • Babur, a Central Asian ruler and a descendant of the Mongol conqueror Genghis Khan invaded India and defeated the Lodi Empire of Northern India.
  • Babur was invited by Daulat Khan Lodi to defeat Ibrahim Lodi.
  • The battle of Panipat was between the armies of Babur and Ibrahim Lodi.
  • Ibrahim Lodi was defeated in the battle and he died in battle along with 15,000 soldiers.
  • Babur won the war and his troops occupied both Delhi and Agra, and the Mughal empire was started.

Additional Information

  • Important battles: 
The first battle of Tarain It was fought in 1191 between Muhammad Ghori and Prithviraj Chauhan
The first battle of Panipat  It was fought between the forces of Babur and Ibrahim Lodhi. The Battle was fought on April 21, 1526.
The second battle of Panipat It was fought between Hindu Emperor Hemu Chandra Vikramaditya and Akbar.  It was fought on 5th November 1556

questions.question: Which of the following dynasties was founded by Qutb ud-din Aibak?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following dynasties was founded by Qutb ud-din Aibak?
questions.solution:
• The Slave dynasty existed in India between AD 1206-1290.
  • Slave Dynasty was established in Northern India by Qutb-ud-Din Aibak, a Turkish Mamluk slave general from Central Asia.
  • In 1206, Muhammad of Ghor, Sultan of the Ghurid Empire, was assassinated.
  • Qutb-ud-Din Aibak became the sultan of Delhi, and that was the beginning of the Slave dynasty.
  • Aibak rose to power when the Ghurid superior was assassinated.
  • He became the ruler of an independent kingdom that evolved into the Delhi Sultanate ruled by the Mamluk dynasty.

questions.question: In which year was the Delhi Sultanate established?
questions.questionHtml: In which year was the Delhi Sultanate established?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is "1206".

Important Points

  • The period between 1206 A.D. and 1526 A.D. in India's history is known as the Delhi Sultanate period.
  • During this period of over three hundred years, five dynasties ruled in Delhi.
  • These were five dynasties as follows:
    • The Slave dynasty (1206-90).
    • Khilji dynasty (1290-1320).
    • Tughlaq dynasty (1320-1413).
    • Sayyid dynasty (1414-51).
    • Lodhi Dynasty (1451-1526).

 

Key Points

  • The Slave Dynasty ruled the Sub-continent for about 84 years.
    • It was the first Muslim dynasty that ruled India. Qutub-ud-din Aibak, a slave of Muhammad Ghori, who became the ruler after the death of his master, founded the Slave Dynasty.
      • He was a great builder who built the majestic 238 feet high stone tower known as Qutub Minar in Delhi. 
    • Razia Begum, the capable daughter of Iltutmush, was the first and the only Muslim lady who ever adorned the throne of Delhi. 
  • Jalal-ud-din Khilji was the founder Khilji dynasty.
    •  Ala-ud-din Khilji was the first Muslim ruler whose empire covered almost the whole of India up to its extreme south.
  • Ghyasuddin Tughlaq, who was the Governor of Punjab during the reign of Ala-ud-din Khilji, ascended the throne in 1320 A.D. and founded the Tughlaq dynasty.

questions.question: Who among the following initiated 'Din-i-Ilahi'?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following initiated 'Din-i-Ilahi'?
questions.solution:
The Mughal Emperor Akbar initiated "Din-i-Elahi".

  • This was meant to combine some of the components of the faiths of his empire, and thereby to resolve the contradictions that separated his subjects. 
  • The components were derived mainly from Islam and Hinduism, although some others were also taken from Buddhism, Jainism and Zoroastrianism.
  • Birbal was the first follower of the Din -i-Elahi.
  • Akbar the Great was the third Mughal emperor to rule from 1556 to 1605. Akbar succeeded his father, Humayun, under the emperor, Bairam Khan.

questions.question: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, raided which famous Indian temple?
questions.questionHtml: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, raided which famous Indian temple?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Somnath Temple, Gujarat.Key Points

  • Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025 AD attacked and looted the Somnath Mandir located in Prabhas Patan near Veraval in Saurashtra on the western coast of Gujarat.
  • Mahmud of Ghazni was the ruler of Afghanistan.
  • The plundered Somnath Mandir was rebuilt by the Paramara king Bhoja of Malwa and the Solanki king Bhimdev I of Anhilwara between 1026 and 1042 AD.
  • Mahmud of Ghazni was a Turkish conqueror who attacked India 17 times between 1000 to 1027 AD.
  • The biggest invasion of Mahmud of Ghazni was in 1025 AD wherein he invaded the Somnath temple in Gujarat.
  • In all his 17 invasions, a number of dynasties were conquered by him.

Additional Information

Temple Location Brief Description
Somnath Temple Gujarat, India One of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines of Lord Shiva, Somnath Temple is a highly revered pilgrimage site for Hindus. This historical temple is said to have been destroyed and rebuilt several times, with the present temple constructed in the Chalukya style of architecture and completed in 1951.
Jagannath Puri Temple Odisha, India This temple is a famous and sacred Hindu pilgrimage site dedicated to Lord Jagannath, a form of Lord Vishnu. The temple is known for its annual Rath Yatra, or chariot festival, in which the three main temple deities are hauled on huge and elaborately decorated temple cars. The current temple structure was built in the 12th century.
Yamunotri Temple Uttarakhand, India Yamunotri Temple is the first stop in the Char Dham Yatra (pilgrimage) of Uttarakhand, dedicated to Goddess Yamuna. It's situated in the Western region of Garhwal Himalayas at an altitude of 3293 meters. The shrine is surrounded by undulating peaks and thermal springs, offering stunning scenic beauty.
Lingaraj Temple Odisha, India This ancient temple, dedicated to Harihara, a form of Shiva and Vishnu, is one of the oldest temples in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. The temple dates back to the 11th century and is a masterpiece of the Orissan style of architecture. The 54.8-meter high central tower dominates the landscape.

questions.question: Which of the following empires was founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following empires was founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the Vijayanagara empire.

Key Points

  •  Harihara I 
    • IN 1336 A.D. Harihara I became the ruler of the Sangama Dynasty
    • He captured Mysore and Madurai.
    • IN 1356 A.D. Bukka-I succeeded him
  • Vijayanagara empire
    • Harihara and Bukka are the founders of the Vijayanagar City in 1336 A.D. on the southern banks of Tungabhadra.
    • They made Hampi the capital city.
    • They served under Vira Ballala III, the Hoysala king.
    • It stretched from the river Krishna in the north to the extreme south of the peninsula.
    • The Vijayanagar Empire was ruled by four important dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu.

Additional Information

  •  Kushan Empire
    • The Kushana Empire or Kushan Dynasty was established by Kujula Kadphises.
    • It was an Indo-European nomadic tribe earlier and was formed by Yuezhi, a group of some Chinese.
  • Chera Empire
    • The Chera dynasty was one of the principal lineages to have ruled over southern India in early history.
    • Cheras controlled the central and northern parts of Kerala and the Kongu region of Tamil Nadu and was a prosperous kingdom owing to its trade with the Romans.
    • The Chera, Cholas, and Pandyas were the most powerful three kingdoms to have ruled during the Sangam Age.
  • Maratha Empire
    • The Maratha Empire dominated a large part of the Indian subcontinent in the 17th century.
    • The empire formally existed from 1674 with the coronation of Chattrapati Shivaji Maharaj and ended in 1818 with the defeat of Peshwa Bajirao II at the hands of the British East India Company.

questions.question: Which of the following musicians of medieval India is referred to as ‘Tuti - e - Hind’ and is also regarded as the father of qawwali?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following musicians of medieval India is referred to as ‘Tuti - e - Hind’ and is also regarded as the father of qawwali?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Amir Khusrau

Key Points

  • Amir Khusrau is often referred to as 'Tuti-e-Hind', which means 'The Parrot of India'.
  • He is also regarded as the father of qawwali, a devotional music form associated with Sufism.
  • Amir Khusrau was a renowned poet, musician, and scholar in medieval India and served in the courts of various rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • His contributions to Indian classical music, including the introduction of new ragas and musical instruments, are highly significant.
  • He is also credited with the invention of the tabla and the sitar.

Additional Information

  • Amir Khusrau was born in 1253 AD in Patiyali, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, India.
  • He was a prolific writer and composed poetry in Persian, Hindavi, and other languages.
  • His literary works include ghazals, masnavis, and riddles, which are still celebrated in South Asian literature.
  • Khusrau's influence on Indian music and culture extends beyond his lifetime, with his legacy continuing to inspire musicians and poets.
  • He played a crucial role in the cultural amalgamation of Persian and Indian traditions during his era.

questions.question: Who built the Hawa Mahal situated in Jaipur?
questions.questionHtml: Who built the Hawa Mahal situated in Jaipur?
questions.solution:
Option 1 is correct, i.e Sawai Pratap Singh.

  • Hawa Mahal, also known as “Palace of Breeze”, was built in 1799 as an extension to the Royal City Palace of Jaipur.
  • In 1799, the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler, Sawai Pratap Singh, grandson of Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh ordered Lal Chand Usta to construct an extension to the Royal City Palace.
  • The five-storeys palace was built in the form of Krishna’s crown because Sarai Pratap Singh was devoted to Krishna, the Hindu god.
  • Jaipur, the current capital of Rajasthan, was built in 1727 AD by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II.

questions.question: During Mughal period, the Sanskrit Mahabharata was translated into Persian as:

questions.solution:
Option 2 is correct, i.e. Razmnama.

  • Razmnama:
    • In Persian, ‘Razm’ means ‘war’, and ‘nama’ means ‘tale’. So, Razmnama means ‘tale of war’.
    • Great Mughal Emperor Jalal Ud-din Muhammad Akbar, commissioned the Mahabharata to be translated into Persian.
    • The translation was carried out by Faizi (brother of Abu’lFazl) and Abd al-Qadir Bada’uni (1540 – 1615).
    • It was under Akbar regime, that the book of Mahabharat was translated in the Persian language.

questions.question: Who ruled over Delhi after Razia Sultan?
questions.questionHtml: Who ruled over Delhi after Razia Sultan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 2. 

Key Points

  • After Razia Sultan, several rulers came to power in Delhi. Here is a list of some of the significant ones:
    • Ghiyasuddin Balban: He was a nobleman in the court of Iltutmish, who later became the Sultan of Delhi in 1266. He was known for his administrative and military reforms and was considered one of the most powerful rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.
    • Muizuddin Qaiqabad: He was the eighth Sultan of Delhi and ruled from 1287 to 1290. He was a weak ruler and was assassinated by his own army commander.
    • Jalaluddin Khilji: He was the founder of the Khilji dynasty and ruled from 1290 to 1296. He was a good administrator and known for his generosity, but his reign was marred by rebellions and revolts.
    • Alauddin Khilji: He was the most famous ruler of the Khilji dynasty and ruled from 1296 to 1316. He was known for his military conquests, administrative reforms, and economic policies.
    • Muhammad bin Tughlaq: He was the Sultan of Delhi from 1325 to 1351. He was a highly educated and intelligent ruler, but his policies were often unsuccessful, and his reign was marked by several rebellions and revolts.
    • These were some of the significant rulers who came to power in Delhi after Razia Sultan.

Additional Information

  •  Shamsuddin Iltutmish was a Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate in India, who ruled from 1211 to 1236 CE. He was born in Central Asia, and was purchased as a slave by Qutbuddin Aibak, the founder of the Delhi Sultanate. Iltutmish rose through the ranks of the Sultanate and became its ruler after the death of Qutbuddin Aibak.

  • Prithviraj Chauhan (1149-1192 CE) was a legendary king of the Chauhan dynasty who ruled from his capital at Ajmer in present-day Rajasthan, India. He is known for his valor, chivalry, and romanticism. Prithviraj Chauhan was born to King Someshwar Chauhan and Queen Karpuri Devi. He was trained in warfare and archery from a young age by his teacher, Chand Bardai, who later wrote the epic poem "Prithviraj Raso" about his exploits.

  • Qutbuddin Aibak was a slave who later became a prominent ruler in the Delhi Sultanate of India. He was born in Central Asia in the late 11th century and was purchased by Muhammad Ghori, a prominent Muslim ruler who was expanding his empire in India. 

    • Qutbuddin Aibak rose to prominence under Muhammad Ghori and was appointed as the governor of Delhi in 1193 CE after the Ghurid conquest of the city.

    • After Muhammad Ghori's death in 1206, Qutbuddin Aibak became the first Sultan of Delhi and established the Slave dynasty, which ruled over parts of northern India for nearly a century.During his reign, Qutbuddin Aibak constructed several important buildings in Delhi, including the Qutub Minar, which is considered to be one of the finest examples of Indo-Islamic architecture.

    • He also built the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, which is the oldest surviving mosque in India.Qutbuddin Aibak died in 1210 CE after falling from his horse while playing polo. He was succeeded by his slave and close confidant, Iltutmish, who went on to establish the Sultanate of Delhi as a major power in India.

questions.questionHtml: Where was Guru Nanak Dev born?
questions.solution:
• Guru Nanak Dev was born on 15 April 1469 at Talwaṇḍi village in the Lahore province of the Delhi Sultanate (present-day Nankana Sahib, Punjab, Pakistan).
  • He was the founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus.
  • Around the age of 55, Nanak Devji settled in Kartarpur and lived there until his death in September 1539.
  • Recently Kartarpur Corridor was opened by the Indian and Pakistan government for the Sikh devotees.
  • The teaching of Guru Nanak Devji can be found in the Sikh scripture Guru Granth Sahib, as a collection of verses recorded in Gurmukhi which was written by Guru Arjan Dev.

questions.question: Whom did Babur defeat at the Battle of Khanwa of 1527?
questions.questionHtml: Whom did Babur defeat at the Battle of Khanwa of 1527?
questions.solution:
•  The Battle of Khanwa of 1527 was fought between Rana Sanga of Mewar and Mughal Emperor Babur after the Battle of Panipat.
  • Rana Sanga was defeated in the war. Babur’s victory consolidated new Mughal dynasty in India.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct order of Dynasty established in India?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is correct order of Dynasty established in India?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is Option 4.

  • Khalji dynasty:
    • It ruled the Indian subcontinent between 1290 and 1320.
    • It was founded by Jalal ud din Firuz Khalji.
  • Tughlaq Dynasty:
    • The rule started in 1320 in Delhi and ended the rule in 1413.
    • Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq was the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty.
  • Sayyid Dynasty:
    • Sayyid dynasty was the fourth dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate and ruled from 1414 to 1451.
    • It was founded by Sayyid Khizr Khan.
  • Lodi Dynasty:
    • It was an Afghan dynasty and ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1451 to 1526.
    • It was founded by Bahlol Lodi.

questions.question: Akbar commissioned ________ to chronicle the story of his father Humayun, 'Humayun-nama'.
questions.questionHtml: Akbar commissioned ________ to chronicle the story of his father Humayun, 'Humayun-nama'.
questions.solution:
• Akbar commissioned Gulbadan Begum to chronicle the story of his father Humayun, 'Humayun-Nama'.
  • She was a Mughal Princess, the youngest daughter of the ruler Babur.
  • She was requested to write the Humayun-Nama by her nephew Akbar.
  • Gulbadan Begum was a very educated woman.

questions.question: _______ was born to the Chauhan King Someshvara and his queen Karpuradevi in 1166 CE.
questions.questionHtml: _______ was born to the Chauhan King Someshvara and his queen Karpuradevi in 1166 CE.
questions.solution:
• Prithviraj Chauhan was born to the Chauhan King Someshvara and his queen Karpuradevi in 1166 CE.
  • He was a Chahamana (Chauhan) King.
  • He controlled much of the present-day Rajasthan, Haryana, and Delhi; and some parts of Punjab, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
  • His capital was located at Ajayameru (modern Ajmer).
  • He repulsed the early invasions by Muhammad of Ghor, a ruler of the Muslim Ghurid dynasty.
  • However, in 1192 CE, the Ghurids defeated Prithviraj at the Second battle of Tarain.
  • Poet and a friend of Prithviraj Chauhan, Chand Bardai wrote Prithviraj Raso giving account of Prithviraj’s reign and personality.

  • Ruler

    Remarks

    Maharana Pratap
    • 13th king of Mewar, Rajasthan
    • Fought tooth and nail to save his kingdom from subjugation by Mughals (Akbar).
    • The Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576 between Maharana Pratap and Akbar's forces led by Man Singh I of Amer.
    • The Mughals were unable to capture Mahrana, and Maharana captured the lost ground soon after.

     Maharaja Suraj Mal
    • Was a Jat ruler of Bharatpur, Rajasthan.
    • He has been described as "the Plato of the Jat people" because of his political sagacity, steady intellect and clear vision.

    Maharaja Man singh
    • Was the last ruling Maharaja of Jaipur State.
    • He ruled the princely state of Jaipur between 1922 and 1949.
    • Was a notable Polo player.

questions.question: Jahangir, the ________ Mughal emperor ruled India from 1605 until his death in 1627.
questions.questionHtml: Jahangir, the ________ Mughal emperor ruled India from 1605 until his death in 1627.
questions.solution:
• Jahangir was the fourth Mughal emperor and his reign lasted from 3 November 1605 to 28 October 1627.

Key Points

  • He was the son of Mughal emperor Akbar and Mariam-uz-Zamani (or Jodha Bai).
  • He was named Salim but on ascending the throne, he adopted Jahangir which means "World Seizer", as his reign name.
  • He was succeeded by his third son, Prince Khurram better known as Shah Jahan.
  • The first Mughal emperor was Babur followed by Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb, and Bahadur Shah Zafar (in the order).

questions.question: Rajataranagini, the book authored by Kalhana in 12 th Century was originally written in which of the following languages?
questions.questionHtml: Rajataranagini, the book authored by Kalhana in 12<sup>th</sup> Century was originally written in which of the following languages?
questions.solution: The Rajtarangini, composed by Kalhana in the 12th century, is a primary historical source on Medieval Kashmir. Written in Sanskrit, it consists of 7826 verses divided into eight books called Tarangas. Kalhana’s father, Champaka, was a minister under King Harsha of Kashmir. The text provides detailed information on the administration, social, political, and economic conditions of the kings of Kashmir. It notably describes the misrule during the reign of King Kalash, son of King Ananta Deva.

questions.question: Who was the fifth guru in Sikhism?

  • The temple is plated with gold.
  • It is built around a Sarovar which was completed by Guru Ram Das in 1577.

questions.question: The city of Victory, Fatehpur Sikri in _________ was built during the glorious reign of the Mughals.
questions.questionHtml: The city of Victory, Fatehpur Sikri in _________ was built during the glorious reign of the Mughals.
questions.solution:
• Fatehpur Sikri is located in Agra district of Uttar Pradesh.
  • The city was founded by Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1571 as the capital of the Mughal Empire.
  • The name of the city can be translated to the 'City of Victory' and was named so after Akbar's successful campaign of Gujarat, the famous Buland Darwaza was also built in honor of the same occasion.

questions.question: Who among the following was defeated in the Battle of Kannauj in 1540?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following was defeated in the Battle of Kannauj in 1540?
questions.solution: The Battle of Kannauj was fought between the Mughal Emperor Humayun and the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri in 1540. Sher Shah Suri emerged victorious in the battle and Humayun was forced to flee to Iran.

questions.question: Which ruler constructed the highest and biggest gateway of Victory, Buland Darwaza?
questions.questionHtml: Which ruler constructed the highest and biggest gateway of Victory, Buland Darwaza?
questions.solution:
• Also known as the "Door of Victory", the Buland Darwaza was built by Mughal emperor Akbar in 1601 A.D.
  • He built the gateway to commemorate his conquest of Gujrat in 1573.
  • It is located 43 km from Agra, as the main entrance to the Fatehpur Sikri complex.
  • It is the highest gateway in the world.

questions.question: Who among the following was defeated by Aurangzeb in the Battle of Deorai?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following was defeated by Aurangzeb in the Battle of Deorai?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Dara Shikoh.

Key Points

  • The battle of Deorai was Fought Between Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh.
  • It was fought in 1659.
  • Dara Shikoh was defeated by Aurangzeb in this Battle.
  • Aurangzeb prisoned his brother Dara Shikoh in Kankawadi Fort (Alwar).

Additional Information

  • Aurangzeb (1658 AD-1707 AD):
    • Aurangzeb defeated Dara at Dharma (1658 AD), Samugarh (1658 AD), and Deorai, in which Samugarh was the decisive one and Deorai was the last one.
    • After the victory, Aurangzeb was crowned at Delhi under the title Alamgir.
    • He died in February 1707 in Ahmadnagar.

questions.question: Badami was the earliest capital of the:
questions.questionHtml: Badami was the earliest capital of the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Chalukyas.

Key Points

  • The earliest Chalukyas with their capital at Badami (Vatapi) in Karnataka.
  • They ruled from mid-6th They declined after the death of their greatest king, Pulakesin II in 642 AD.
  • They were known as Badami Chalukyas.

Additional Information

  • Chalukya Rulers:
  • Jayasimha was the first ruler of the Chalukyas.
  • Pulakesin I (Reign: 543 AD – 566 AD)
    • Founded the empire with his capital at Vatapi.
    • Performed Ashwamedha.
  • Kirtivarman I (Reign: 566 AD – 597 AD)
    • Son of Pulakesin I.
    • Conquered Konkan and northern Kerala.
  • Mangalesha (Reign: 597 AD – 609 AD)
    • Brother of Kirtivarman I.
    • Conquered the Kadambas and the Gangas.
    • Was killed by his nephew and son of Kirtivarman, Pulakesin II.
  • Pulakesin II (609 AD – 642 AD)
    • The greatest of the Chalukya kings.
    • Extended the Chalukya rule to most parts of the Deccan.
    • He is famous for stopping Northern king Harsha in his tracks while he was trying to conquer southern parts of the country.
    • He had defeated the Pallava king Mahendravarman I but was defeated and killed by Mahendravarman’s son and successor Narasimhavarman I in a series of battles he had with the Pallavas.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs is associated with the taxation system of the Marathas?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following pairs is associated with the taxation system of the Marathas?
questions.solution:
Chauth and Sardeshmukh are associated with the taxation system of the Marathas.

Key Points

  • Chauth was a daily tax or tribute levied by the Maratha Empire, from the beginning of the 18th century. This was a nominally levied annual tax on profits or output at 25 percent.
  • It was levied on the lands that were under Mughal nominal control.
  • The sardeshmukh was on top of the chauth an extra 10 percent tax.
  • It was initiated by Koli Maharaja Som Shah of Ramnagar.

Additional Information

questions.question: Who among the following rulers is related to “market regulatory measures” in medieval India?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following rulers is related to “market regulatory measures” in medieval India?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is Alauddin Khilji.

  • Alauddin Khilji is related to “market regulatory measures” in medieval India.
  • He has adopted price regulation steps for a wide range of products on the market.
  • Alauddin's courtier, Amir Khusrau, and the writer of the 14th century, Hamid Qalandar, say that these reforms were made by Alauddin for public welfare.
  • Barani claims, however, that Alauddin decided to reduce the prices in order to make his soldiers low wages appropriate, and therefore to retain a large army.
  • Alauddin appointed market supervisors and spies to ensure that the goods were sold at controlled rates, and received independent reports from them.
  • His administration barred farmers and traders from storing grains to prevent a black market and built government-run granaries where the government's share of the grain was stored.
  • In order to enable rapid grain transport to Delhi, the government also forced transport workers to resettle at distinct distances along the Yamuna River in villages.

questions.question: The mausoleum of the Taj Mahal was designed by _______________.
questions.questionHtml: The mausoleum of the Taj Mahal was designed by _______________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Ustad Ahmad Lahori

Key Points

  • Ustad Ahmad Lahori is credited with being the principal designer of the mausoleum of the Taj Mahal.
  • The Taj Mahal, an iconic symbol of India, is located in Agra and was commissioned by Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
  • The construction of the Taj Mahal began in 1632 and was completed in 1653.
  • It is renowned for its stunning architecture, intricate carvings, and the use of white marble.
  • The Taj Mahal is a UNESCO World Heritage site and attracts millions of visitors from around the world each year.

Additional Information

  • The Taj Mahal is considered one of the greatest achievements in Mughal architecture.
  • It combines elements from Islamic, Persian, Ottoman Turkish, and Indian architectural styles.
  • The structure's white marble exterior reflects varying hues according to the light conditions, giving it a different appearance at different times of the day.
  • The surrounding gardens and reflective pools further enhance the beauty of the Taj Mahal.
  • In addition to being a symbol of love, the Taj Mahal is also a testament to the rich cultural heritage and architectural prowess of the Mughal era.

questions.question: Along which river bank among the following did the ancient city of Madurai, the capital of Pandya Kingdom, exist?
questions.questionHtml: Along which river bank among the following did the ancient city of Madurai, the capital of Pandya Kingdom, exist?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Vaigai.

Key Points

  • River Vaigai
    • Madura, the later capital of Pandyas was the central seat of Tamil Sangam literature.
    • Today, Madurai is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities.
    • Madurai was located on the banks of River Vaigai in Tamil Nadu.

Additional Information

  • Pandya dynasty
    • It is also known as the Pandyas of Madurai, was a dynasty of south India, one of the three famous Tamil lineages, the other two being the Chola and the Chera
    • The dynasty passed through two periods of imperial dominance, the 6th to 10th centuries CE, and under the 'Later Pandyas' (13th to 14th centuries CE).
    • The Pandyas ruled extensive territories, at times including the large portions of present-day south India and northern Sri Lanka through collateral branches subject to Madurai.
    • The rulers of the three Tamil dynasties were referred to as the "three crowned rulers (the mu-ventar) of the Tamil country".
    • The age and the antiquity of the Pandya dynasty are difficult to establish.
    • The early Pandya chieftains ruled their country (the Pandya Nadu) from time immemorial, which included the inland city of Madurai and the southern port of Korkai

questions.question: Mehrunnisa who was known as Nur Jahan was the wife of ______.
questions.questionHtml: Mehrunnisa who was known as Nur Jahan was the wife of ______.
questions.solution:
Mehrunnisa who was known as Nur Jahan was the wife of Jahangir.

  • Jahangir was the son of Mughal emperor Akbar.
  • He ruled from 1605 until his death in 1627, for 22 years.
  • The popular Shalimar Bagh in Srinagar was built by Jahangir.
  • It is in his time when paintings culture flourished in India.
  • Jahangir died in Kashmir.

questions.question: The ________ is a Jain text containing the biographies of the Jain Tirthankaras, most notably Parshvanath and Mahavira.
questions.questionHtml: The ________ is a Jain text containing the biographies of the Jain Tirthankaras, most notably Parshvanath and Mahavira.
questions.solution:
• The Kalpa Sutra is the Jain text containing the biographies of the Jain Tirthankaras, most notably Parshvanath and Mahavira.
  • Kalpa Sutra was written by Bhadrabahu who was in the court of Chandragupta Maurya.
  • The first Tirthankara of Jainism was Rishabhdev and he is also known as Rishabhanatha and Adinatha.
  • Lord Mahavir  was the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism and regarded as the true founder of Jainism.
  • Parshvanath was the 23rd Tirthankaras of Jainism.

questions.question: The Peacock Throne was commissioned by _________.
questions.questionHtml: The Peacock Throne was commissioned by _________.
questions.solution:
• The Peacock Throne was commissioned by ​Shah Jahan in the early 17th century.
  • It was the seat of Mughal Emperors in India and was placed in the Diwan-i-Khas in the Red Fort of Delhi.
  • When Nadir shah attacked and looted India in 1739, he also took the precious throne with him.
  • The Peacock Throne was covered in gold and jewels, with steps leading up to it, with the ruler floating above the ground.
  • The opulence and magnificence can be estimated from the fact that it cost twice as much as the construction of the majestic Taj Mahal.
  • The peacock throne had the famous Koh-I-Noor diamond embedded in it.
  • Extra:-
  • Babur was the founder and the first ruler of the Mughal Empire in India.
  • He defeated the Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
  • Famous ruler chronologically is- Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jehangir, Shah jahan, and Aurangzeb.
